newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU health chief attacks tobacco industry.
newsitem.headline: EU health chief attacks tobacco industry.

text.p: European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn renewed his attack on the tobacco industry on Friday, condemning a cigarette price war as a ploy to lure new smokers in the face of publicity bans.

"This is a cynical attempt by the tobacco companies to recruit new smokers, which also reflects the increasing constraint on other marketing strategies," Flynn said in a statement to mark annual World No-Tobacco Day on Saturday.

Flynn, the EU's top health official, said he was "very concerned" about a price war producing fierce competition between leading manufacturers including Britain's Imperial Tobacco and Gallaher Ltd and U.S. giant Philip Morris .
A squeeze on advertising has seen cigarette firms increasingly resorting to price cuts, promotions, direct- marketing campaigns and prize draws to keep their top selling brands in the public eye.
Flynn hailed plans by Britain's new Labour government for a national ban on tobacco ads and sponsorship of sports events.
Britain's announcement has raised Commission hopes of getting a total EU-wide ban on cigarette ads, after five years of resistance from a blocking minority of EU governments.
Flynn is to put the issue to EU health ministers on June 5.
The Irish commissioner's criticism of the price war is his fourth direct attack on the tobacco companies in the last two years.

He criticised Philip Morris in 1995 for running newspaper adverts declaring that smoking bans infringed personal liberty and that measures requiring smokers to respect the rights of non-smokers were unreasonable.

Flynn said that 30 percent of all cancers were tobacco related, smoking caused three million deaths per year worldwide and six major studies had concluded passive smoking increased the risk of lung cancer, heart disease and childhood asthma.

The running battle flared up again last June when Philip Morris launched a major advertising campaign saying scientific evidence showed that exposure to second-hand smoke was less dangerous than drinking whole milk or eating biscuits.

"The public should greet this message with the scorn it deserves," Flynn fumed, saying the campaign was "evidence of panic in the tobacco industry at the threat posed to tobacco sales by concerns over passive smoking".

The Irishman also crossed swords with colleagues last December, after Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler rejected calls to end EU subsidies for tobacco production, for fear of job losses among 200,000 tobacco-related workers.
